newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Hong Kong comes to terms with handover.
newsitem.headline: China's Hong Kong comes to terms with handover.

text.p: Super-capitalist Hong Kong took the switch to communist China rule in its stride on Tuesday -- most people appeared to have come to terms with their fate as new Chinese citizens.
"I'm definitely happy, I've been waiting for this to happen for years. They are here to liberate us from the British," said retiree Mang Kam, 74, as he waved a miniature Chinese flag.
Britain handed this wealthy cosmopolitan city back to China at midnight on Monday, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
Beijing quickly dispatched a 4,500-strong force of the People's Liberation Army, combining land, air and sea elements with an impressive armoury.
In a grand show of force, 21 armoured personnel carriers (APCs) rolled into an army camp in the heart of Hong Kong's Tsim Sha Tsui shopping belt. But no-one appeared to be alarmed.
"Why are we so enthusiastic? Maybe it's because we finally rule ourselves now," said Mang's friend.
Mang and his friend were among more than 500 people who waited for more than two hours in driving rain on Tuesday morning to cheer the entry of the Chinese troops.
Elsewhere, Hong Kong people, famous for their entrepreneurial skills, were riding high on the China enthusiasm.

In a burst of retrospective-chic, some store assistants sported Chairman Mao caps or the red scarves made popular by China's young Red Guards during the radical leftwing Cultural Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s.
Patriotic mainland songs wafted from some shops to provide customers with in-store entertainment.

Even the young appeared to be coming to terms with their new rulers. Some young school children marked the occasion of Hong Kong's first day as a Chinese region by taking time off from the five-day public holiday to return to school to sing China's national anthem and raise its flag.
"A hundred and fifty years of humiliation and shame have been washed clean," said a primary school principal, who sang the anthem with over a dozen pupils.
Some remained worried about life under communist rule, however.
"I'm really going to miss the British soldiers, I am just so afraid the Chinese soldiers will have no regard for the law," said Jenny Li, 24, an executive with a European firm.
